By means of the physical marks of the *saṃbhogakāya* (retribution body) on the level of fruition, they illuminate and clarify. First, the question: "Are the marks of the *saṃbhogakāya* Buddha as great as Sumeru, the king of mountains?

The answer is: "They are exceedingly great. Regarding Sumeru, this is translated as "Wondrously High" (*Miaogao*). It is called "wondrous" because it is composed of the four jewels, and it is called "high" because it rises above all other peaks.
It is said: "High. This explains the reason for its greatness. When the Buddha says it is "not a body," it is because its original nature is empty;
that which is thus called a "great body" is precisely the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*).
"Subhūti, suppose there were as many Ganges Rivers as there are grains of sand in the Ganges River. What do you think?
Would the sands of all those Ganges Rivers be numerous? Subhūti replied, "They would be very numerous, World-Honored One.
Those Ganges Rivers alone would already be countless, let alone their sands. Subhūti, I now tell you this in truth: if...

“Suppose there were a son of good family or a daughter of good family who, with the seven precious jewels, filled as many trichiliocosm worlds as there are grains of sand in those Ganges Rivers and used them as a gift.
Would they gain much merit? Subhūti replied, “Very much, World-Honored One.
The Buddha told Subhūti, “If a son of good family or a daughter of good family, within this sutra, were to even receive and uphold four [lines...]"
and expounds it for others—even a single verse or gāthā—this merit shall surpass the former merit.

Furthermore, Subhūti, wherever this sutra is spoken, even as little as a single four-line verse, you should know that this place should be honored by the entire world, including its devas, humans, and asuras, as if it were a stupa or shrine of the Buddha;
how much more so for one who is able to receive, uphold, and recite it in its entirety?
[Sūtra] Subhūti, you should know that such a person accomplishes the most supreme, foremost, and rare dharma.
Wherever this sūtra resides, there is a Buddha, as well as his honored disciples.

This passage on the comparative excellence of the merit of upholding and expounding [this sutra] serves to manifest the superiority of the sutra itself. It follows the preceding section on the absence of attainment and non-existence.
Even if one were to fill a great trichiliocosm with the seven treasures and offer them as a gift, it would not equal the merit of upholding this sutra.
"All these worthy sages and saints have their distinctions based on the unconditioned dharma. This concludes the passage.

Even if one were to fill as many great trichiliocosm worlds as there are grains of sand in the Ganges River with the seven treasures and give them as alms, it would not equal the merit of upholding this sutra.
As the meaning of the sūtra becomes increasingly profound, its comparative evaluation becomes increasingly superior. The initial question concerns counting the sands by means of many rivers:

"If every grain of sand in the Ganges River were itself made into a Ganges River, would the total number of grains of sand in all those 'Ganges-river' channels be great? The answer was: "Extremely great."

Next, he asked: "To illustrate the merit of giving by means of many rivers—if someone were to fill with the seven treasures as many worlds as there are grains of sand in the Ganges River and give them as a gift, would they obtain much merit? He replied, "Very much. The Buddha told Subhūti:
"To manifest the superiority of this sutra by means of great merit—if someone were to receive and uphold even a single four-line verse of this sutra..."
And to explain it for others—their merit surpasses that [of the former]. Zhongfeng said: "Giving with the seven treasures does not avoid the arising of the mind and dwelling upon signs;
upholding the Prajñāpāramitā results in nothing arising in the mind and nothing dwelling upon signs; therefore, its merit is superior."

Not only is the merit of those who briefly uphold this sūtra exceptionally sublime, but the place where this sūtra is briefly upheld should be venerated by all devas and humans as if it were a stūpa of the Buddha.
In the Sanskrit language, *stūpa* means "square mound"; *tā* refers to...

The dialects of frontier lands are corrupt. "Temple" (*miao*) refers to appearance; enshrining the Buddha’s *śarīra* is called a "stūpa," while enshrining the Buddha’s physical image is called a "temple.

The phrase "how much more so for those who... and below speaks of the benefits for one who extensively upholds this sutra—not merely a single four-line verse, but being able to receive and uphold it entirely.
One should know that such a person accomplishes the most supreme, foremost, and rare Dharma. This means they have attained it.
*Prajñāpāramitā*. It accomplishes the unsurpassed fruit of Buddhahood and Bodhi. The following clarifies the location where this entire sūtra resides:

it is fully endowed with the Three Jewels, and thus there is a Buddha. This sūtra reveals the Dharmakāya; based upon the Dharmakāya, there exist the Saṃbhogakāya and Nirmāṇakāya. As stated previously:
All Buddhas, as well as the Dharma of the Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi of all Buddhas, all emerge from this sutra.
If one respects the disciples, it is because the sutra reveals the unconditioned (asaṃskṛta), and based upon the unconditioned, there are the three vehicles (triyāna).
As previously stated: "All worthy sages have distinctions based upon the dharma of non-action (*asaṃskṛta-dharma*).
At that time, Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying: "World-Honored One, what should this sutra be named?
How should we receive and uphold it? The Buddha told Subhūti: "This sutra is named the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā*. By this name..."
"Memorize this, Subhūti; you should uphold it. Why is that? Subhūti, what the Buddha calls 'prajñāpāramitā' is not actually prajñāpāramitā;
it is merely designated as 'prajñāpāramitā. Subhūti, what do you think?"
"Does the Tathāgata have any dharma that he has taught? Subhūti replied to the Buddha, "World-Honored One, the Tathāgata has not taught any dharma.
"Subhūti, what do you think? Are all the atoms contained within the trichiliocosm many?
Subhūti said, "Very many, World-Honored One. "Subhūti, those atoms which the Tathāgata has spoken of, the Tathāgata has said they are not atoms."
"Dust. This is called "minute dust. The Tathāgata says that what is called a "world" is not a world;
this is called a "world. Subhūti, what do you think? Can the Tathāgata be seen by means of the thirty-two marks? "No, World-Honored One.
The Tathāgata cannot be seen by means of the thirty-two marks. Why is this? The Tathāgata says that the thirty-two marks are..."

These are the marks; these are called the thirty-two marks. Subhūti, if there were good sons or good daughters who were to give away their lives as many times as there are grains of sand in the Ganges River in acts of charity, and if there were another person who, from within this sutra, were to receive, uphold, or even recite a single four-line verse for others, the latter’s merit would be far greater.
This passage clarifies that there is no fixed dharma to be spoken. Having heard that upholding this sutra accomplishes such rare dharmas, Subhūti asked:
"What is the name of this sutra? How should it be upheld? The Buddha told him it is named the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā*.
By means of *prajñā*, one illuminates and shatters the two attachments to self and phenomena (*ātma-dharma-grāha*), realizing that saṃsāra is itself nirvāṇa.
Pán: Delusions are themselves bodhi. This is like saving sentient beings without a self, or the intention of practicing giving without dwelling on signs.
Because its essence is firm, the myriad things cannot destroy it. As the Book says: "Is it not called 'firm'? It may be worn down by grinding, yet it does not become thin."

Furthermore, it is said: "The higher one looks up at it, the higher it seems; the harder one drills into it, the harder it proves. Zhuangzi said: "Though a great flood reaches the heavens, he is not drowned;

though a great drought melts metal and stone, and a single mountain is scorched, he does not feel the heat. It is because his functioning is so sharp that he is able to transform all things. The Book of Documents says:
"Be without intentionality, without necessity, without stubbornness, and without self. It also says: "Overcome the self and return to principle. Because of this...

It possesses the two meanings of "firmness" (*dṛḍha*) and "sharpness" (*tīkṣṇa*), and is therefore likened to a *vajra*. One employs names that do not abide in fixed characteristics to uphold the meaning within those names.
An objection is raised: "For what reason does one uphold the meaning within the name? The explanation states: "Because within the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*), there are no names;

thus it is 'not [merely] prajñā'. The *Awakening of Faith* says: "It is free from the characteristic of verbal expression, free from the characteristic of names, and free from the conditions of the mind."
Regarding these characteristics, Laozi said: "The Way that can be spoken of is not the eternal Way; the name that can be named is not the eternal name.
The nameless is the beginning of heaven and earth. Zhaorun said: "Things have no reality that corresponds to their names, and names have no efficacy to grasp things.

That things have no reality corresponding to their names means they are not [true] things; that names have no efficacy to grasp things means they are not [true] names. Name and reality are non-existent..."
"When all things are present, where do they abide? Like the horns of a rabbit or the hair of a tortoise, these are all names for things that are actually non-existent.
This is what is called *prajñā*. The Profound Discourse (*Xuántán*) says: "In profound stillness, one forgets words; yet the waves and ripples of the ocean of teachings are vast and overflowing.

Fearing that Śūnyatā-putra had not yet realized that the nature of *prajñā* is emptiness, and might thus assume there were verbal teachings, he asked the Tathāgata whether any Dharma had been preached.
Since Śūnyatā-utpanna (Kōngshēng) had realized that names are themselves nameless, he understood that explanations are themselves non-explanations. He replied: "The Tathāgata has nothing to explain.
It is like a great bell waiting to be struck: struck hard, it rings loudly; struck lightly, it rings softly; if not struck, it does not ring.
At the very moment it is struck, there is fundamentally no sound; yet even when it is not struck, it has never been without sound.
Yongjia said: "Speaking when silent; silent when speaking. The Great Gate of Giving is opened, without obstruction.
Below this, he proceeds to compare the world-systems with the number of their atoms, asking Subhūti, "Are they many? He replied, "Very many. The Buddha said:
Since it is said that "it is precisely not Prajñā," then it is not atoms and not worlds.
Since it is said that "it is designated as Prajñā," then it is designated as atoms and designated as worlds. Because one is empty, all are empty; because one is such, all are such.
This correctly reveals that there is no fixed dharma to be spoken of. Master Han said: "This clarifies that in every land and at every atom..."
All of these are the wondrous essence of Vairocana, which perfectly accords with the Great Master Xuelang, like two halves of a tally fitting together.

Previously, when it was said that one should not dwell upon signs while practicing giving, this was clarified by means of the *nirmāṇakāya* (response body). Next, when it was said that no fixed dharma can be obtained, this was clarified by means of the *saṃbhogakāya* (recompense body).
Now, regarding the statement that no fixed dharma can be preached, he again questions [the Buddha] concerning the thirty-two marks. The answer says:
Since it has been stated that they are not prajñā, not atoms, and not worlds, it says: "This is the absence of marks.
Since it has been stated that these are named prajñā, named atoms, and named worlds, it says: "These are named the thirty-two marks.

Below, the text uses internal wealth as a comparison to further manifest the superiority of this sutra, such as when Śākyamuni, during his causal stage, sacrificed his body to feed [a starving tigress].
The tiger [Vishvantara] cut his own flesh to substitute for the pigeon, going so far as to sacrifice his head, eyes, marrow, and brain. The *Lotus Sūtra* states: "Observe the trichiliocosm;
there is not even a space the size of a mustard seed that is not a place where a bodhisattva has sacrificed his body and life."

Suppose there were someone who, with as many bodies and lives as there are grains of sand in the Ganges, practiced giving. The merit thereby obtained would not equal the superior merit of upholding this sutra.
That sacrifice of body and life is abiding in signs; it constitutes a cause for outflows (*āsrava*). To uphold and expound this sutra is non-abiding in signs;

At that time, Subhūti, upon hearing this sutra being preached, deeply understood its meaning and intent; he wept with tears of sorrow and addressed the Buddha, saying:

When the mind is pure, the true mark (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*) arises. You should know, World-Honored One, that such a person accomplishes the foremost and most rare merit.
World-Honored One, this true mark is itself a non-mark; therefore, the Tathāgata speaks of it by the name "true mark.
World-Honored One, for me now to hear such a sutra as this and to believe, understand, accept, and uphold it is not difficult. But if, in a future age...
In the final five hundred years, there may be sentient beings who hear this sutra, believe and understand it, and accept and uphold it. Such persons are truly the most rare and extraordinary.
Why is this? Because these people are without the mark of a self (*ātman*), the mark of a person (*pudgala*), the mark of a being (*sattva*), or the mark of a life-span (*jīva*).
And why is that? Because the mark of a self is precisely no-mark; the marks of a person, a being, and a life-span are likewise no-marks.
[The Buddha said: “Characteristics. Why is this? To be free from all characteristics is precisely what is called the Buddhas.

This passage explains the meaning of the non-existence of speech regarding the cause that gives rise to this emptiness. Having heard the Buddha’s teaching on Prajñāpāramitā, [Subhūti] realized that it is “not Prajñāpāramitā”;
thus he deeply understood its profound significance and, moved by the Buddha’s deep kindness, wept with tears of sorrow, saying: “The Great Matter has already been accomplished.”
"Clear! It is as if one were mourning for one's deceased parents. Regarding the praise of the Buddha’s rarity:

previously it was said he was rare, yet although we had seen the World-Honored One’s wondrous qualities, we had not heard this teaching. Now that we have received this exposition, he is truly rare. Below, the reason for his rarity is set forth:
the Buddha says that even this profound scripture is "not Prajñā-pāramitā. We of the Lesser Vehicle merely distance ourselves from the four marks.

Having already attained the emptiness of persons (*pudgala-śūnyatā*), yet not being free from the marks of phenomena (*dharma-nimitta*) and thus not having attained the emptiness of phenomena (*dharma-śūnyatā*), they have not been able to hear this sutra.
They do not realize that the Buddha expounds the Dharma with a single voice, yet sentient beings each attain understanding according to their own kind.

Those among the assembly of the *Avataṃsaka* who, though possessing ears, did not hear the Perfect and Sudden Teaching—these are precisely such people as these. This is because of the nature of the Dharma...
There is no difference; it is simply that their capacities are distinct. As the Book says: "Of the Master's Way, who was the first to transmit it? Who was the last to grow weary of it?
It is like plants and trees—their categories are already distinguished. Only the Sage can encompass both the beginning and the end.
Suppose there were someone who, upon hearing this sutra, attained pure faith; they would immediately give rise to the true mark (bhūtalakṣaṇa), which is utterly genuine.

Absence of delusion is called faith. When faith arises from one’s own mind, one returns to place faith in one’s own mind; within this mind, one has faith that there is fundamentally no self or dharmas.
This is termed "purity," whereby one accords with the wondrous mind of true reality (*bhūtatathatā*). Therefore, it is said that one immediately gives rise to true reality.
As for true reality: all marks are markless, and marklessness is not a mark. All marks being markless, one does not abide in birth-and-death; marklessness...
It is neither [existent nor non-existent]; it does not abide in nirvāṇa; it is neither being nor non-being. It wondrously accords with the Middle Way. The *Lotus Sūtra* says:
"Only Buddhas and Buddhas can exhaustively fathom the true reality (*dharmatā*) of all phenomena. The *Treatise* says: "The cause of the Mahāyāna is the true reality of all phenomena;
the fruit of the Mahāyāna is likewise the true reality of all phenomena. It further says: "The initial resolve and the ultimate [attainment]—these two..."

They are not distinct. Thus, between these two minds, the former mind is difficult [to realize]. The arising of the true mark (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*) is the cause; the accomplishment of the foremost, most rare merit is the fruit.
Since the preceding text already stated, "It is precisely not Prajñā," why does it further state, "It is precisely the arising of the true mark"?
This is because although gold dust is precious, if it falls into the eye it becomes a speck of dirt; [the text speaks thus] in order to eliminate the discriminating mind regarding the true mark.
Therefore it is said: "This is precisely the absence of marks. The *Perfect Enlightenment Sūtra* states: "I shall cause all to enter ultimate perfect enlightenment;

To say that I, Ajita, have already attained the fruit of sainthood (*āryaphala*), and that when the Buddha was present it was not yet the age of the final dharma (*paścimakāla*), such that hearing this sutra, being able to believe in one's own mind, understanding the meaning of the true mark, and receiving and upholding it without loss—this is not difficult.

Suppose there are sentient beings who, though they have not yet attained the fruits of sainthood, hear this sutra and believe, understand, accept, and uphold it.

The nature of the self; this nature of the self is identical and in union with the Tathāgata. As it was said previously: "If one sees that all marks are non-marks, one then sees the Tathāgata.

The first *pāramitā* is not, in fact, the first *pāramitā*; it is called the "first *pāramitā*" [only] by way of designation.
Subhūti, the *pāramitā* of patience, the Tathāgata says, is not the *pāramitā* of patience; it is called the "*pāramitā* of patience" [only] by way of designation.

"O Sage, throughout all those worlds, there was no mark of a self, no mark of a person, no mark of a sentient being, and no mark of a life-span.

How much more so for those whose faith is pure, and who believe, understand, accept, and uphold it? Hereafter, the person is illustrated by means of the Dharma.
When the Tathāgata speaks of the "foremost pāramitā," he means that among all the perfections (*pāramitā*), Prajñā is supreme.
Because one must be able to understand this Prajñā, such a person is also rare. Yet, Prajñā is not Prajñā; the foremost is not foremost.
This is called "the foremost" because it is a conventional designation. To elaborate further: patience (*kṣānti*) is not actually patience.

To endure is called patience; to be harmed is called insult. Because one can endure all insults, it is named "patience through endurance" (*kṣānti*). If there were a subject who endures and an object that is endured, [it would not be true patience].

If one clings to the four marks, it is not called a *pāramitā*. When one does not perceive a subject that endures nor an object that is endured, and remains far removed from the four marks, it is therefore called a *pāramitā*.
Fearing that sentient beings might cling to these words without understanding, [the Buddha] sweeps away the traces by saying: "It is precisely not patience."

Because it endures both the object and the subject [of harm], it is called patience (*kṣānti*). It is so designated through conventional designation (*prajñapti*). Below, the "patience accomplished in a single lifetime" is cited:
"While I was practicing the path of patience during my causal stage, there was a King Kali—here translated as 'Extremely Wicked'—who, having grown weary from hunting, fell asleep.

A palace attendant paid homage to the seer (*ṛṣi*). The king became enraged and asked the seer, 'Have you attained the four fruits [of the śramaṇa]? All replied, 'We have not. [Thereupon, the king] cut [the seers] to pieces."
[The sage’s] limbs [were struck]. The heavens rained down stones in anger. The King, fearing this, repented. The Immortal was originally without anger;
the King likewise had no intent to harm. The Immortal’s body remained as it was before. At that time, I did not possess the four marks. [This is explained in reverse:
Had I possessed the four marks at that former time, anger and resentment would have arisen. Since anger and resentment did not arise, we know there is no self. An ancient said: "When..."
Facing a blade held to one's head is just like cutting the spring breeze. Laozi said:
"One who skillfully preserves life is such that the rhinoceros has nowhere to plant its horn, the tiger has nowhere to set its claws, and the soldier has no place to apply his blade. Why is this?

Because such a person has no ground of death. He extensively cited how, throughout five hundred past lifetimes, he had cultivated the practice of patience and remained far removed from the four [grounds of fear].
This is due to the power gained from prajñā.
Therefore, Subhūti, a bodhisattva should give rise to the mind of anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi while remaining detached from all marks.
One should not give rise to the mind by dwelling on form; one should not give rise to the mind by dwelling on sound, smell, taste, touch, or dharmas. One should...

"A Bodhisattva’s mind should not dwell on form when practicing giving. Subhūti, for the sake of benefiting all sentient beings, a Bodhisattva should practice giving in this manner.

Subhūti, if a bodhisattva dwells upon dharmas while practicing giving, it is like a person entering into darkness.

Then there is nothing seen. If a bodhisattva practices giving with a mind that does not dwell on phenomena, it is like a person with eyes who, when the sunlight shines brightly, sees all manner of forms.

One should not allow the mind to dwell upon the six sense objects; thus one is free from all marks (*lakṣaṇa*). One should give rise to a mind that dwells nowhere; this is precisely all dharmas.
When the mind arises without dwelling, and when the arising of the mind is non-dwelling, then there is neither "identity" nor "separation," and one is unattached to both.

The arising of selflessness—these two characteristics are like the inside and outside of a vessel. Fearing that those who have not yet given rise to faith in emptiness might be skeptical, he exhorts them with these five phrases:

Without doubt. Furthermore, because that which is attained within the mind is neither real nor unreal, one speaks in accordance with principle:
appearance is non-appearance, and arising is non-arising. As the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* states: "The Tathāgata knows and perceives the characteristics of the triple world as they truly are."
Neither real nor unreal; neither identical nor different. "Neither real" means that when one is empty, all are empty. "Neither unreal" means that when one is suchness, all are suchness.
"Neither identical" means that it is empty yet not empty. "Neither different" means that it exists yet does not exist.
It was stated previously: "There is no fixed dharma by which one attains bodhi; there is no fixed dharma that can be taught.

"Seeing" refers to the blind, which is a metaphor for wisdom that lacks the illumination of principle. "In the darkness there is no sunlight" is a metaphor for the absence of remedial dharmas;
thus, one cannot perceive the true reality (*dharmatā*) of all phenomena. The following clarifies the attainment of non-abiding in marks:

if a bodhisattva’s mind does not abide in the six sense objects while practicing giving, it is like a person with eyes—this is a metaphor for possessing the wisdom that illuminates principle. "The sunlight" [is the illumination of the sun].
When illumination shines, darkness is extinguished; this is a metaphor for attaining the method of counteraction. To see various forms is to see the true reality (*dharmatā*) of all phenomena.
The preceding section has concluded the refutation of the characteristics of phenomena (*dharma-lakṣaṇa*).

In this manner, he gives away his body for immeasurable hundreds of thousands of myriads of koṭis of kalpas. Yet, if there should be another person who, upon hearing this sutra, believes it with faith and does not oppose it, [the merit of the latter would be far greater].
The merit of that person would be superior to theirs. How much more so for one who writes it down, receives and maintains it, recites and reads it, and explains it to others!
Subhūti, to state the essential point: this sutra possesses inconceivable, immeasurable, and boundless merit.

The Tathāgata has taught it for those who have set out upon the Great Vehicle; he has taught it for those who have set out upon the Supreme Vehicle. If there is anyone who can receive, maintain, and read...
Recite it and explain it extensively for others. The Tathāgata fully knows these people; the Tathāgata fully sees these people.
They shall all achieve immeasurable, incomparable, boundless, and inconceivable merit.
Such people as these are indeed carrying the burden of the Tathāgata’s *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*. Why is this? Subhūti, if...
Those who delight in inferior dharmas are attached to the view of a self, the view of a person, the view of a sentient being, and the view of a life-span.
Consequently, they will be unable to hear, receive, read, recite, or explain this sutra to others. Subhūti, wherever this sutra may be found—
One should know that this place is a stūpa worthy of being honored by all the world—gods, humans, and asuras;
it should be revered, saluted, and circumambulated, and one should scatter various flowers and incense upon that spot.
This is the section clarifying the supreme excellence of the merit of upholding this sutra. First, it clarifies the attainment of the Buddha’s knowledge and vision;

its merit is precisely that which was previously described as the accomplishment of the most supreme and rare dharma. Below, the text provides a comparative evaluation of the blessings of upholding the sutra.
The first two instances concern external wealth; the third concerns internal wealth, referring only to the giving away of one’s body and life as numerous as the sands of the Ganges.
Now, this fourth instance concerns the giving away of bodies and lives as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, three times every day, throughout many kalpas.
"The first period" refers to the morning; "the middle period" refers to midday; and "the latter period" refers to the afternoon.
Even for a long duration— where "many" refers to lifetimes and "great" refers to significant matters, and "long" refers to the passing of kalpas—
the merit obtained would still not equal the merit of believing in this sutra, let alone the merit of receiving, upholding, explaining, and elucidating it.
The following reveals that the Dharma is supreme and the person is honored; it describes the inconceivable merit of this sutra.

"Inconceivable" means that the dharma which is free from marks cannot be thought upon by the mind or discussed through words, just as the empty space of the ten directions cannot be conceived by the mind or debated with speech.
"Unmeasurable" means that it cannot be designated by words or measured by the intellect. "Boundless merit" refers to...

Because it accords with the nature of reality and is boundless, its merits are likewise infinite. When the Tathāgata speaks for those who have set out in the Mahāyāna, even the followers of the two vehicles cannot reach it;
when he speaks for those who have set out in the supreme Buddha-vehicle, it is not within the realm of the three stages of worthiness.
Thus, only the Buddha’s knowledge and vision can recognize a person who is able to uphold and expound this sutra, as such a person has accomplished the inconceivable.

Regarding this merit: such a person is one who carries the fruit of Buddhahood and Bodhi upon their back. To carry on the back is called "bearing" (*he*); to carry on the shoulder is called "shouldering" (*dan*).
All Buddha-dharmas emerge from this sutra; it is like a heavy burden. One who is able to give rise to the Great Mind then bears and carries it with their entire being.
As the verse says: "Before the empty kalpa, there was the Shadowless Tree; supporting heaven and propping up earth, its bare branches stand stark and tall."
In Xinzhou there was a wood-seller who gathered his load and carried it on a pole. Cheng asked, "For what reason do you carry and recite this sutra?

He replied, "It is precisely for the sake of bearing the burden of Bodhi. Cheng said, "If those of the Two Vehicles delight in inferior dharmas and perceive the existence of principle and phenomena through cultivation and realization, they are attached to the four views and cannot receive, uphold, explain, or interpret this sutra."
The "four views" refer to the aforementioned four characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*). Because one clings to views, one clings to characteristics;

since the characteristics are themselves the views, by now delighting in the Great Dharma and being free from these four views, one is able to shoulder the burden of Bodhi. The following clarifies the excellence of the locus in order to manifest the excellence of the person.
Whether in the heavens or among humans, wherever this sutra exists, the eight classes of devas and nagas should all offer it worship.
Although there may be no stupa, it is as if there were one; for it contains the Dharma-body and the relics of the Buddha, and thus one should pay homage to it and scatter flowers as an offering.
Long ago, there was a skilled scribe who transcribed the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra* in mid-air. A woodcutter...
Whenever the herdsman sought shelter from the rain, they all turned toward his location. He constantly heard the sound of celestial music.

Later, a monk from India passed by and saw this, asking, "Who has written the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra* here? Only then did he realize that this was proof of the previous person’s transcription of the sutra;
though there were no traces left in the air, the music still played as an offering. How much more so, then, for a place where the entire scripture resides—how could it not be honored?
They are honored by devas and nāgas.

Furthermore, Subhūti, if a son of good family or a daughter of good family who upholds, recites, and studies this sutra is treated with contempt by others, it is because of their karmic offenses from previous lives which would have caused them to fall into the evil realms;
yet, because they are now treated with contempt by people in this life, those [offenses]... [are exhausted].
Worldly sinful karma will then be extinguished, and one shall attain Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.

nor by a thousandth, ten-thousandth, or ten-millionth part, nor even by any calculation, number, or analogy can it be reached.
Subhūti, if sons of good family or daughters of good family, in the final age at the end of time...

This clarifies the passage concerning the transformation of heavy [karma] into light.

This person’s past unwholesome karma would have caused them to fall into the three evil realms; however, by upholding and reciting this sutra, their heavy offenses are transformed into a light retribution.

They shall receive only the reward of being slighted and despised in this present life, whereby all their past heavy karmic debts are completely extinguished, and they shall attain the fruit of Buddhahood and Bodhi.

This is a doubt. The following provides a summary: "One should know that the meaning of this sutra is inconceivable" because it was spoken by the Tathāgata for those who have set out upon the Great Vehicle, and for those who have set out upon the supreme Buddha-vehicle.
