When one has thus saved all sentient beings to their end, one perceives no further birth.

"One may deliver them. [The Master] immediately brought his mind down to the state of non-self. [The student] questioned him, saying: "When a Bodhisattva delivers sentient beings, there must be a subject who transforms and an object that is transformed;
one must transcend birth-and-death and realize nirvana. Why do you say that no sentient beings exist to be delivered? He explained:

"If one perceives that there are sentient beings to be delivered, then one possesses the four marks [of self, person, being, and life], and is not a Bodhisattva. As the Sūtra says: "All sentient beings are within the hearts of the Buddhas."
When mind after mind realizes Buddhahood, one no longer perceives the sentient beings who are to be transformed, the Bodhisattva who transforms them, or the Nirvana that is realized.
Zhang Zhuo said: "Nirvana and birth-and-death are equal to flowers in the sky. A questioner asked:

"For what reason is it said that having a self is not being a Bodhisattva, while being without a self is called being a Bodhisattva? The explanation states: "If there were any dharma through which one could give rise to the bodhicitta, [then one would still perceive such distinctions]."
If there were the mark of a self, one could not give rise to the bodhicitta because phenomena do not exist; if there is no mark of a self, who then can deliver sentient beings?
Subhūti, what do you think? Did the Tathāgata obtain any dharma from the Buddha Dīpaṃkara by which he attained Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi?

“Did [the Tathāgata] attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*? “No, World-Honored One. As I understand the meaning of what the Buddha has taught, there is no dharma by which the Buddha attained *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* while in the presence of Dīpaṃkara Buddha.
The Buddha said, “So it is, so it is, Subhūti. Truly, there is no dharma by which the Tathāgata attained *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.”

"Subhūti, if there were any dharma that the Tathāgata had attained as anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, then Dīpaṃkara would not have bestowed upon me this prediction: 'In a future age, you shall become a Buddha named Śākyamuni.
Because, in reality, there is no dharma by which one attains anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, therefore—"
Dīpaṃkara Buddha conferred upon me this prediction, saying: "In a future age, you shall attain Buddhahood;
your name shall be Śākyamuni.
This clarifies the passage concerning how there is no dharma within the causal stage that attains bodhi. As stated previously, one generates the mind of bodhi through the absence of dharmas.
If that were so, there would be no Bodhisattvas. How then could Śākyamuni have cultivated the practices of a Bodhisattva?
Therefore, he cites the principle of abiding in Bodhi through non-attainment to clarify that there is no dharma by which one generates the Bodhicitta, and no birth that can be delivered.

First, he cites the meaning of the non-attainability of any dharma within the causal stage to question Subhūti: "When the Tathāgata was with the Buddha Dīpaṃkara, was there any dharma by which he attained Bodhi?"
"Is it not so? "It was indeed so. Dīpaṃkara was the Buddha whom Śākyamuni encountered during the second asaṃkhyeya kalpa.
Subhūti replied: "The youth Sumati attained no dharma at the place of Dīpaṃkara Buddha that constituted his awakening.
The Buddha praised him in this way, saying that his understanding was unerring. At the place of Dīpaṃkara Buddha, there was truly no dharma by which he attained [awakening]."
Enlightenment (*bodhi*). Since afflictions are themselves enlightenment, and the nature of afflictions is empty and unobtainable, then enlightenment is likewise unobtainable.
[The following] provides an inverse explanation: "If there were any dharma that I could obtain, then Dīpaṃkara would not have bestowed a prediction upon me.
[The following] provides the direct explanation: "Because there is no dharma that can be obtained, he bestowed a prediction upon me. In the Sanskrit language, Śākyamuni—this...
It is said that "Able Man (Nengren) is tranquil and still," which expresses the meaning of responding through transformation to the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*).

If one discusses the state of ultimate reality (*bhūtatathatā*), there is neither prediction nor non-prediction; yet, within the realm of partiality, there is indeed the conferring of predictions (*vyākaraṇa*). An ancient saying goes:
"The ten thousand pipes have hearts, yet no one can hear them; the solitary crag has no ears, yet it knows its own resonance."
Why is this? "Tathāgata" means the suchness (*tathatā*) of all dharmas.
Subhūti, if someone were to say that the Tathāgata has attained *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, Subhūti, in reality there is no dharma that the Buddha has attained as *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
Subhūti, as for the *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* attained by the Tathāgata...
Subhūti, herein there is neither reality nor unreality. Therefore, the Tathāgata says: "All dharmas are Buddha-dharmas.
Subhūti, that which is called "all dharmas" is precisely not all dharmas; it is for this reason they are called "all dharmas."
“Subhūti, it is as if there were a person with a large body. Subhūti said, “World-Honored One, when the Tathāgata speaks of a person with a large body, that is precisely not a large body;
it is merely designated as a ‘large body.’”
This clarifies the passage stating that no dharma can be attained as enlightenment within the fruit [of Buddhahood].

To say that enlightenment cannot be attained within the cause implies that there are no Buddhas or Tathāgatas in the fruit; therefore, it is said: "The Tathāgata is the meaning of the emptiness of all dharmas.
Because the emptiness of all dharmas is named the Tathāgata, the *Heart Sūtra* says: "All these dharmas have the characteristic of emptiness," and the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* says: "The nature of form..."

"True Emptiness" (zhēnkōng) first precludes erroneous interpretations. If someone were to say that the Tathāgata attains bodhi upon the fruition [of the path], such a person does not understand the meaning of what I have taught.
Below, the correct view is shown: "In reality, there is no dharma by which one attains bodhi"; this is precisely the meaning of the suchness (tathatā) of all dharmas.
Below, it is further explained: furthermore, fearing that someone might give rise to slander—if one says there is no attainment, then one falls into nihilism (uccheda).
It is extinguished. Therefore it is said: "The Bodhi attained by the Tathāgata is neither real nor unreal. 'Neither real' means it is not existent; 'nor unreal' means it is not non-existent.
To say it exists is the view of eternalism; to say it does not exist is the view of nihilism. To say it both exists and does not exist is a contradictory view;
to say it neither exists nor does not exist is a view of conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*). As the ancients said: 'It is beyond the four propositions.'"
Severing all hundredfold negations, I entreat the Master to point directly to the meaning of the Western Coming. As it was said previously: "There is no fixed dharma by which one attains bodhi.
Yet this *tathatā* (suchness) does not possess a separate essence; it is precisely all dharmas. Neither existent nor non-existent, they are all the Buddha-dharma.
The *Prabhāsa-sūtra* says: "Space is boundless; know that *prajñā* (wisdom) is likewise boundless. Form is boundless..."
Know that Prajñā is also boundless. An ancient said: "The lush green bamboo is nothing other than the true suchness (tathatā) realm of Prajñā;
the dense yellow flowers are all the wondrous provisional mind of Bodhi. To sweep away these traces below: it is not that all phenomena exist;
they are without reality, yet this is called "all phenomena. They are without falsehood. One should previously abide in the absence of any fixed phenomenon to be grasped.

Having finished reading the text, [the Buddha] considered that the *saṃbhogakāya* (reward body) could not be used to manifest the teaching. Now, having subdued [Māra], there is no *bodhi* (enlightenment) to be attained;
thus, considering that the *dharmakāya* (dharma body) could not be used to manifest the teaching, he asked Subhūti: "All dharmas are indeed Buddha-dharmas."
This is the essence of *tathatā* (suchness), which pervades all places; it may thus be called "great. Śūnyatā-janman replied:

"The *dharmakāya* is vast and grows great, yet because it is far removed from all marks (*lakṣaṇa*), it is called 'not a great body. That which is called the 'great body' is so named because *tathatā* is indestructible."
Subhūti, it is the same for a bodhisattva. If one were to say, "I shall bring immeasurable sentient beings to parinirvāṇa," that person would not be called a bodhisattva.
Why is this? Subhūti, there is truly no dharma that can be named "bodhisattva.
Therefore, the Buddha has said that all dharmas are without self, without person, without sentient being, and without life-span. Subhūti, if...
If a bodhisattva were to say, "I shall adorn the buddha-fields," he would not be called a bodhisattva. Why?
The Tathāgata has said that what is called "adorning the buddha-fields" is in fact no adorning; it is merely named "adornment.
Subhūti, if a bodhisattva penetrates the non-existence of self and phenomena, the Tathāgata declares him to be a true bodhisattva.
This passage clarifies the text concerning the non-existence of beings who can be saved. It was stated previously that Śākyamuni has no *bodhi* to be attained;
thus, one should know that there is no dharma for generating the *bodhicitta*, nor are there any sentient beings to be saved. Therefore it says: "The Bodhisattva is also like this.
If one were to say, 'I shall save sentient beings,' then one possesses the four marks and is not called a Bodhisattva. This is because [in reality] there are none.

There is a dharma that is far removed from the four marks; this is called a bodhisattva. Because it is a non-dharma, the Buddha taught that for all bodhisattvas and sentient beings, there are no four marks.
This is clarified by citing the matter of adorning buddha-fields while abiding in the Middle Way:
if one perceives a field as something that can be adorned, one is attached to the four marks and is not called a bodhisattva. Because there is no field...
It may be adorned; therefore it is said that "it is not adornment," yet it is called "adornment" because it is conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*).
Below, there is a double conclusion: since there are beings to be delivered and lands to be adorned, one is not [truly] a bodhisattva. Why? What is called a bodhisattva?
If a bodhisattva penetrates the mark of non-self and the mark of dharmas, he is truly a bodhisattva.
"Subhūti, what do you think? Does the Tathāgata possess the fleshly eye? "Yes, World-Honored One, the Tathāgata possesses the fleshly eye.
"Subhūti, what do you think? Does the Tathāgata possess the divine eye? "Yes, World-Honored One, the Tathāgata possesses the divine eye.
"Subhūti, what do you think? Does the Tathāgata possess the wisdom-eye? "Yes, World-Honored One..."
“Venerable One, the Tathāgata possesses the wisdom-eye (*prajñā-cakṣus*). Subhūti, what do you think? Does the Tathāgata possess the Dharma-eye (*dharma-cakṣus*)?
“Yes, World-Honored One, the Tathāgata possesses the Dharma-eye. “Subhūti, what do you think? Does the Tathāgata possess the Buddha-eye (*buddha-cakṣus*)?
“Yes, World-Honored One, the Tathāgata possesses the Buddha-eye. “Subhūti, what do you think? Regarding the Ganges River...”
“Are all the grains of sand therein sand? “Yes, World-Honored One; the Tathāgata says they are sand.
“Subhūti, what do you think? Suppose there were as many Ganges Rivers as there are grains of sand in one Ganges River.”
"As many as there are grains of sand in all those Ganges Rivers, so many are the Buddha-worlds. Would these not be very many?
"Very many, World-Honored One. The Buddha told Subhūti: "In all those lands, the Tathāgata fully knows the various kinds of minds of all sentient beings.
Why is this? The Tathāgata says that all minds are 'no-minds'; it is for this reason that they are called 'minds'."
Why is this? Subhūti, the past mind cannot be apprehended; the present mind cannot be apprehended;
the future mind cannot be apprehended.
This clarifies that the Buddha possesses the five eyes, and thus knows all sentient beings—this refers to the passage beginning with "which are not, in fact, sentient beings. Part One.
Question: Does the Tathāgata possess the fleshly eye (*māṃsacakṣus*)? Answer: The Tathāgata possesses the fleshly eye; this applies likewise up to the Buddha-eye (*buddhacakṣus*).

The fleshly eye sees forms within obstructions; this refers to ordinary worldlings (*pṛthagjana*). The divine eye (*divyacakṣus*) sees forms beyond obstructions; this refers to those who have attained the four fruits [of the śramaṇa].
Aniruddha attained a divine eye that covered half his head, and he observed the great trichiliocosm as if it were in the palm of his hand.
The *āmra* fruit. The Buddha attains the "whole-head" divine eye (*divyacakṣus*), which perceives through and through the countless worlds among humans without dualistic characteristics.

The wisdom-eye (*prajñācakṣus*) is the fundamental gnosis (*mūla-jñāna*) that illumines ultimate truth. Regarding the stage of the pratyekabuddha and the provisional rank of the bodhisattva, it is the dharma-eye (*dharmacakṣus*).

Regarding the stage of the *samyaksambodhi-samantaka* (Equal Enlightenment), it is the subsequently attained gnosis (*prsthalabdha-jñāna*) that preaches the Dharma to deliver sentient beings. These four eyes prior [to the Buddha's final realization] are collectively termed the "Buddha-eye" when residing in a Buddha.
The eye sees the Buddha-nature as perfectly complete. Regarding this, Yunyan asked Dawu, "What is the use of the Great Compassionate Bodhisattva having so many hands and eyes?
Dawu replied, "It is like a person at midnight reaching back with their hand to feel for their pillow. Yunyan said:
"I understand. Daowu asked, "How do you understand it? Yankong replied, "My whole body is hands and eyes. The *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* says:
"The eighty-four thousand mudrā-arms and the eighty-four thousand pure jewel-eyes are all within a single thought-moment of the person.
Regarding the passage that follows, "What do you think? it uses a single Ganges River as a measure to count its sands. As [the sands are infinite]...
Take one Ganges River; take the sands of one river to count all such rivers; take the sands within all those rivers to count all world-systems (*dhātu*);
take all the lands within those world-systems to count all beings within those worlds;
and take the various kinds of minds within each being—their inverted conceptualizations and their distinctions of defilement and purity—to count every single mind of every sentient being.
The *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* says: "Whatever they contemplate, whatever they ponder, and whatever they cultivate—the Tathāgata knows them all, because he is of one essence with them.
The *Śūraṅgama-samādhi-sūtra* says: "You should know that within this world of outflows, the twelve classes of beings possess the wondrous clarity of fundamental enlightenment;
this perfected essence of the awakened mind is no different and not distinct from the Buddhas of the ten directions. The *Avataṃsaka-sūtra* says: "If a person..."

If you wish to know the realm of the Buddha, you should purify your mind so that it is like empty space. Stay far removed from discursive thoughts and all forms of grasping, so that wherever the mind turns, there is no obstruction.
Although *prajñā* is non-cognitive, there is nothing it does not know. If one speaks of the five eyes, they should be called "seeing.
Why, then, is it called "knowing"? It is like a blind person gazing into the darkness; the seeing does not reside in the eye. And yet...

It resides within the mind; there has never been a perception external to the mind. It is merely designated as "seeing" in relation to the eye, and "knowing" in relation to the mind, for they possess no dual substance.
Why is it that [the Tathāgata] knows all? The Tathāgata taught that the nature of all minds is empty of false conceptualization;
therefore, he says they are "not-mind. Because True Suchness (*tathatā*) is indestructible, he says this is called "mind. The following explains why it is "not-mind": the past has already ceased.
It does not abide in the present; it has not yet arisen in the future. Seeking it throughout the three periods of time, it is utterly unfindable.

Subhūti, what do you think? If someone were to fill a trichiliocosm with the seven treasures and give them as a gift, would that person, by reason of this, acquire much merit? "So it is, World-Honored One. That person, by means of this..."
For this reason, the merit obtained is exceedingly great. Subhūti, if merit were substantial, the Tathāgata would not say that one obtains much merit;
because merit is non-existent, the Tathāgata says that one obtains much merit.
This passage clarifies that the nature of merit is empty. Previously, it was stated that there is no land to adorn and no beings to deliver;
thus, even giving would yield no merit. Therefore, the emptiness of the nature of merit is now explained in detail. First, the question:
"If a person were to fill a great trichiliocosm with the seven treasures and give them as a gift, would that person, by reason of this, obtain much merit? The answer is: "Yes."
Because this person practices giving free from signs and without inversion, they obtain immense merit.
The Buddha and Śāriputra clarify that if merit were substantial, one would dwell in signs, resulting in the cause of outflows (āsrava), and thus the merit would be meager.

Because the nature of merit is empty, one is free from signs, resulting in the cause of non-outflows (anāsrava), and thus the merit is vast. The following three sections provide a comparative analysis.
Regarding the scriptural passage: these are all mentioned here for the sake of convenience.
Subhūti, what do you think? Can the Buddha be seen by means of his body of perfect physical form? "No, World-Honored One."
The Tathāgata should not be perceived by means of the body of perfect form. Why is this?
The Tathāgata has said that the body of perfect form is itself not a body of perfect form; it is merely designated as "the body of perfect form. Subhūti, what do you think?
Can the Tathāgata be perceived by means of the possession of the various marks? "No, World-Honored One. The Tathāgata should not be perceived by means of the possession of..."
One perceives various marks. Why is this? The Tathāgata has said: "To be fully endowed with all marks is itself not being fully endowed; it is merely called 'being fully endowed with all marks.

This clarifies the passage stating that the Buddha’s body is not composed of marks. Since it was previously stated that there is no bodhi to be attained, how could there be the primary and secondary marks?
Therefore, it is explained that he is "not" [a Buddha] despite being fully endowed with clarity. The Sūtra says: "The Tathāgata is the meaning of the suchness (tathatā) of all dharmas.
It also cites the passage concerning how one should dwell so as to be able to see the Tathāgata by means of the thirty-two marks:
"The fully endowed physical body" refers to the eighty secondary characteristics; "the fully endowed various marks" refers to the thirty-two primary marks. These are "not" [merely] fully endowed.
Goodness is itself without goodness; marks are themselves without marks. When the Buddha was in the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven preaching the Dharma for his mother, he descended to the human realm.
The bhikṣuṇī Utpalavarṇā transformed herself into a Wheel-Turning King and went first to see the Buddha.
The Buddha said, "Śūnyatā was sitting in tranquil meditation within a mountain cave; she saw me first. He further said, "If a person, for hundreds of thousands of kalpas, constantly follows..."
The Tathāgata does not perceive a reality apart from the ultimate truth; those who are blind and do not see the Buddha are called "those who possess [the truth].
Delusion has no inherent nature; its entire substance is itself the Real.
Subhūti, do not think that the Tathāgata has this thought: "I shall preach some dharma. Do not have such a thought. Why is that?
If anyone were to say that the Tathāgata has preached some dharma, they would be slandering the Buddha, for they would not understand what I have preached.
Subhūti, as for one who preaches the Dharma, there is no dharma that can be preached; it is called "preaching the Dharma" only by way of designation.

This clarifies the passage concerning the non-existence of any dharma that can be taught. Since it was previously stated that the Buddha is fundamentally without marks, how could he preach the Dharma?

Therefore, this is clarified by means of the principle that no dharma exists that can be taught. It also cites the passage stating that one should abide in the realization that there is no fixed dharma to be taught.
First, to prevent misunderstanding: You must not think that the Tathāgata has the thought, "I shall preach the Dharma. Do not entertain such a thought.
If anyone says that the Tathāgata has preached the Dharma, they slander the Buddha;
for the Tathāgata preaches without preaching, and preaches while there is no preaching. If one says there is preaching, they do not understand the meaning of what the Tathāgata has preached.
The following demonstrates right view. Regarding the one who preaches the Dharma: there is no dharma that can be preached, like an echo responding in an empty valley.

Without mind and without conditions, free from all conceptual discrimination, one speaks all day long yet never speaks at all. As the *Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra* says: "There has been no preaching, there is no present preaching, and there will be no future preaching;
that which is not preached is the Buddha's preaching. As Laozi says: "His words fill the world, yet he commits no verbal transgression. This is it.
He is called a "preacher of the Dharma" because he expounds it according to the capacities of beings without hindrance.
At that time, the Venerable Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying: "World-Honored One, will there be any sentient beings in future ages who..."
"Upon hearing this Dharma, will they give rise to faith? The Buddha said, "Subhūti, they are not sentient beings, yet they are not non-sentient beings.
Why is that? Subhūti, as for 'sentient beings,' the Tathāgata has said they are not sentient beings; they are merely designated as 'sentient beings.'"
This is the passage clarifying that sentient beings are not [truly] sentient beings. As it was previously stated: "There is no bodhi; there is no mark;

there is no teaching. Therefore, the question is asked regarding future sentient beings as to whether they will be able to give rise to faith upon hearing this sutra, thereby manifesting the sense of its being difficult to believe.
The Buddha clarifies this by means of "no sentient beings," intending to manifest that there is faith. That they are "not sentient beings" is because their fundamental nature is empty;
that they are "not non-sentient beings" is because of the aggregation of the five aggregates. Regarding "sentient beings, sentient beings," the *Shorter Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra* says:
The text of this reiterated statement is as follows: "World-Honored One, World-Honored One; Bodhisattva, Bodhisattva," and so forth.
Regarding why sentient beings are called "sentient beings," I say that they are not sentient beings because they lack the characteristic of a composite entity.

That they are nevertheless called "sentient beings" is because conventional designations are not destroyed. As previously stated: "In truth, there are no sentient beings who attain parinirvāṇa. Furthermore—
Previously, the meaning of the non-existence of sentient beings was not clarified; next, the unobtainability of the three minds was clarified;
now, the unobtainability of the mark of a sentient being is clarified, thereby manifesting the true sense that there are no sentient beings. As Śāriputra asked the goddess Prajñākūṭā:
"Why do you not transform this female body? The goddess replied: "If one seeks the mark of a woman, it is utterly unobtainable."
Furthermore, it is like the dragon girl who, in a mere instant, transformed into a male and immediately went to the stainless world in the south,
where she sat upon a precious lotus flower and attained equal and perfect enlightenment. How can one make distinctions based on such characteristics as male or female,
old or young, good or evil, or ordinary person or sage?

Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying, “World-Honored One, when the Buddha attains *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, is it that there is nothing to be attained? The Buddha said, “So it is, so it is, Subhūti.
Regarding my *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, there is not even the slightest dharma that can be attained; this is called *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.”
The three types of awakening. Furthermore, Subhūti, this dharma is equal; it has no high or low.

This is called *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*. By practicing all wholesome dharmas without a self, without a person, without a sentient being, and without a life-span, one attains *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*. Subhūti, as for what is called "wholesome" [dharmas]...
"Regarding 'Dharma,' the Tathāgata says it is not a dharma; therefore, it is called 'good dharma.

This clarifies the passage concerning the non-attainment of bodhi. Subhūti realized that there is no mark, no teaching, and no arising, and understood that there is no dharma by which one attains bodhi.
Therefore, he first presented his understanding by clarifying that the name 'unsurpassed' is bodhi, stating that the Buddha attains bodhi."
"Is it because there is nothing to be attained? The Buddha confirmed and praised this, saying: "There is not the slightest dharma that can be named 'bodhi.
That which is called 'not the slightest dharma' refers to the bodhicitta. When deluded, one transmigrates through the six realms, yet it has never diminished.
As the *Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra* says: "Transforming the thirty-two marks, it enters into the bodies of all sentient beings, like a precious gem covered in grime."
Though wrapped in garments, upon awakening, one transcends worldly toil; yet it has never increased. The Sixth Patriarch said:
"Bodhi originally has no tree; the bright mirror is also not a stand. Originally there is not a single thing—where could dust settle?
Next, he clarifies that the name "Perfect Equality" is Bodhi. This Dharma is equal, with no high or low; that which is named Bodhi is the *dharmadhātu*.
Within the nature [of reality], there is no form and no characteristic; it is utterly without differentiation, and is therefore called "equality.
Because of this equality, one does not regard the Buddha as high or sentient beings as low. Free from the characteristics of subject and object, it is vast and traceless;
thus it is said that there is no high or low. An ancient said: "The Buddhas of the past were thus. The seven groups of four in the Western Heaven and the two [patriarchs] in the land of Tang..."
The three patriarchs were likewise so; such-and-so [the disciple] was likewise so. Sengzhao said:

"If all dharmas are not different, how could one say that they are made non-different by lengthening the webbed feet of a mandarin duck or shortening the neck of a crane? Nor is it by leveling mountains or filling valleys that they become non-different.

It is simply that although the webbed feet of the duck are short, one feels distress at lengthening them; and although the neck of the crane is long, one feels grief at shortening it. One must simply allow the high to remain high and the low to remain level."
It remains level where it is low. Where it is long, let it be long; where it is short, let it be short. The verse says: "Let it be short or let it be long, there is no need for cutting or patching;
wherever it is high or low, it naturally levels itself. The following clarifies that true awakening is called *bodhi*.

Because it is free from the four marks (*catur-nimitta*), one attains *bodhi* by cultivating all wholesome dharmas (*kuśala-dharma*). As stated previously: "There is not even the slightest dharma... and so forth.

The Dharma is equal; yet, fearing that people might fall into the deep pit of nihilism—where there is neither cultivation nor realization, and where one repudiates the six perfections and myriad practices—an ancient said:
"Though it be the old hall and empty fields, only after winning them back once will you finally rest."
Therefore it is said: "There are no four marks; one cultivates all wholesome dharmas. The *Awakening of Faith* states:
"Although one knows that the nature of phenomena is fundamentally free from stinginess and greed, one practices the *dāna-pāramitā* and other perfections in accordance with this truth.

This subsequently sweeps away all traces. Since there is no bodhi, how could there be wholesome dharmas? Therefore it is said: "They are not wholesome dharmas. Through the illusory transformation of Buddha-works, cultivation is itself non-cultivation.
These are called wholesome dharmas from the perspective of conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*).

Subhūti, suppose there were someone who took all the Sumeru kings of mountains within a trichiliocosm and offered them as a heap of the seven precious jewels as a gift; yet, if another person were to take this *Prajñāpāramitā* Sūtra...
Even as little as a four-line stanza, if one receives, upholds, reads, recites, and explains it to others, the previously mentioned merit does not equal even a hundredth part of it;
it does not equal a hundred-thousand-million-billionth part, nor can it be reached by any calculation or analogy.

This passage compares the merit of upholding this sutra: if one were to take the seven treasures of Mount Sumeru throughout a great trichiliocosm and offer them as a gift, it would be a cause for outflow (sāsrava);
its merit would still be meager. To uphold and expound even a single four-line verse of this sutra is a cause without outflow (anāsrava), and its merit is immeasurable.
Subhūti, what do you think? You should not think that the Tathāgata has this thought: "I shall deliver sentient beings.
Subhūti, do not have such a thought. Why is that? Because in reality, there are no sentient beings whom the Tathāgata delivers.
If there were any sentient beings whom the Tathāgata had delivered, the Tathāgata would possess a self, a person, a sentient being, and a life-span.
Subhūti, when the Tathāgata says "there is a self," it is not that there is a self; yet ordinary people imagine there is a self.
Subhūti, those who are called ordinary persons by the Tathāgata are, in truth, not ordinary persons; they are merely designated as "ordinary persons.
This clarifies the passage stating that there is no birth for the Tathāgata to deliver.

Since it was previously said that "this Dharma is equal, with no high or low," how could the Tathāgata have any birth to deliver? Therefore, it is said: "You should not say that the Tathāgata acts..."

Regarding the thought of saving sentient beings: you all should not harbor such a thought. Previously, it was said that the three minds are unattainable, and it was also said that the mark of sentient beings is empty;
how, then, could there be any sentient beings to be saved? If one perceives that there are sentient beings to be saved, the Tathāgata would likewise be attached to the four marks.
Although the Tathāgata speaks of a self, fundamentally there is no self; yet ordinary people take this to be so.

There is a self. Since sentient beings are not truly sentient beings, and ordinary persons are not truly ordinary persons, they are called "ordinary persons" because the five aggregates are a provisional combination.
The preceding text has thus completed its mutual refutation of the mark of a self and the mark of dharmas.
“Subhūti, what do you think? Can the Tathāgata be perceived by means of the thirty-two marks?
Subhūti replied, “So it is, so it is. The Tathāgata can be perceived by means of the thirty-two marks.
The Buddha said, “Subhūti, if the Tathāgata were to be perceived by means of the thirty-two marks, then a Wheel-turning Sage King would also be a Tathāgata. Subhūti addressed [the Buddha]:
The Buddha said, "World-Honored One, as I understand the meaning of what the Buddha has taught, one should not perceive the Tathāgata by means of the thirty-two marks.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke these verses:
"To see me by form, or to seek me by sound—such people follow a deviant path and cannot perceive the Tathāgata.
This clarifies the text stating that the Dharma-body cannot be seen through marks. As previously stated: "It cannot be [seen] by means of the marks of perfection."
[Subhūti] wishes to see the Tathāgata. Looking downward, he intends to shatter the marks of non-Dharma; therefore, he cites the first thirty-two marks to pose a question.
He awaits Subhūti’s response to see [the Buddha] through these marks, which would mean abiding in conventional sentiment. Not seeing [the Buddha] through marks, one falls into nihilism.
His initial question—“Can the Tathāgata be perceived by means of the thirty-two marks?”—is precisely the World-Honored One’s probe.
The pole is in his hand; the shadow and the grass follow him. Unless one examines it with one's own hands and eyes, one cannot avoid falling into the Buddha’s trap.
Śāriputra replied, "It is so. One knows by means of inferential knowledge (*anvaya-jñāna*).

One may perceive the Tathāgata through the thirty-two marks, just as one knows there is fire upon seeing smoke from behind a mountain. Once the marks are understood as being no-marks (*animitta*), then one may..."
[Subhūti] judged the Tathāgata by means of his physical marks. The Buddha challenged him with the difficulty that ordinary beings and sages are not distinguished [by marks].

"If one perceives the Tathāgata by means of marks, then a Cakravartin King who possesses the thirty-two marks would also be a Tathāgata. Although the Cakravartin King possesses the thirty-two marks, he does not understand that they are not marks;
because he is an ordinary being, Subhūti (Kūṭadanta) turned back at a single stroke, which accorded with the principle.
In response: One should not perceive the Tathāgata by means of physical marks. The Buddha’s seal is beyond seeing and hearing.
If one perceives the Dharma-body through form, or seeks the Dharma-body through sound, this is practicing a deviant path; one does not see the Tathāgata.
For the physical body is not the Buddha, and the same applies to sound. An ancient said: "The Layman Dongpo is far too talkative. Sound—
One desires to pass through the thicket of forms. If the stream is sound and the mountain is form, then with neither mountain nor water, one is filled with sorrow.
Subhūti, if you should think that the Tathāgata has attained Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi by means of marks that are fully complete...
[attains] *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*. Subhūti, do not have such a thought. It is not by means of the possession of marks that the Tathāgata has attained *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
Subhūti, if you were to have such a thought—that those who resolve to attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* preach the annihilation and extinction of all phenomena—do not have such a thought.
Why is this? One who has resolved to attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* does not speak of the characteristic of annihilation regarding phenomena.
This clarifies the passage concerning non-abiding in the characteristic of annihilation. As previously stated, one cannot perceive the Tathāgata by means of signs; although...
He does not abide in existence. Furthermore, fearing that the person might give rise to emptiness and fall into the view of nihilism, he addressed him before he had even asked:
"If you should think, 'The Tathāgata did not attain bodhi because of his marks of perfection,' do not entertain such a thought."
The Tathāgata does not attain Bodhi by means of the marks of perfection; yet, he is also not apart from form and sound, for one perceives the Buddha’s supernormal powers therein.
As东坡 (Dongpo) said: "The sound of the stream is itself the broad and long tongue; the color of the mountains is nothing other than the pure body.
The eighty-four thousand gāthās of last night—how can they be recounted to others on another day? This concludes the section clarifying the refutation of marks.
This is an error. If one conceives the thought of generating the bodhicitta while asserting that all dharmas are subject to annihilation, do not entertain such a thought.

Sengzhao said: "It is like fleeing from a mountain peak only to rush into a valley; in both cases, one cannot escape suffering. For what reason does generating the mind not involve the doctrine of annihilation?
Because a person who has generated the bodhicitta should not speak of the characteristic of annihilation regarding dharmas. As the saying goes:

It would be better to give rise to a view of existence as large as Mount Sumeru than to give rise to a view of emptiness based on overweening pride (*adhimāna*). The preceding section concludes the refutation of the characteristics of non-dharmas.

Subhūti, if a bodhisattva were to take the seven treasures filling worlds as numerous as the sands of the Ganges and offer them as a gift, [the merit would not equal that of one who understands this Dharma].
Furthermore, Subhūti, if there is another person who knows that all dharmas are without self and attains patience (*kṣānti*), this bodhisattva surpasses the merit obtained by the former bodhisattva.
Why is this? Subhūti, it is because these bodhisattvas do not accept meritorious blessings (*puṇya*).
Subhūti said to the Buddha, “World-Honored One, why does a bodhisattva not accept merit?
“Subhūti, a bodhisattva should not be greedily attached to the merit they have performed; for this reason, it is said that they do not accept merit.”
This is a passage comparing the superior merit of a bodhisattva who has attained *kṣānti*.

If a bodhisattva were to fill worlds as numerous as the sands of the Ganges with the seven treasures and offer them in charity, it would not equal the superior merit of a bodhisattva who has attained *kṣānti*, because there is a difference between that which possesses marks and that which is markless.
"Kṣānti" here refers to the *anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti* (the patient acceptance of the non-arising of phenomena). As stated previously: it cannot be...
To see the Tathāgata as having marks is not to see that there is arising; to see the Tathāgata as being without marks is not to see that there is cessation.
To accept this dharma of neither arising nor cessation within the mind is called the "patience of non-arising" (anutpattika-dharmakṣānti).
This is the stage of the Bodhisattva dwelling in the first ground (*prathamabhūmi*). Previously it was said:

"If a Bodhisattva penetrates the non-existence of self and phenomena (*anātma-dharma*), the Tathāgata calls him a true Bodhisattva. It was then questioned: "For what reason is the merit of a Bodhisattva who knows non-self so exceptionally superior?
It is because the Bodhisattva does not accept the characteristics of merit (*puṇya-lakṣaṇa*). Subhūti asked again: "Since a Bodhisattva already possesses the characteristics of merit..."

"What does it mean to 'not accept'? The Buddha said: "One should not greedily grasp at or become attached to the marks of the merit produced by a bodhisattva, nor give rise to views of annihilationism or eternalism. For this reason, it is said that one does not accept merit."
Subhūti, if anyone were to say that the Tathāgata comes or goes, sits or lies down, that person does not understand the meaning of what I have taught.
Why is this? The Tathāgata comes from nowhere and goes nowhere;
therefore, he is called the Tathāgata.
This is the passage clarifying that the Dharmakāya has no characteristics of coming or going. It was stated above that by knowing all phenomena are without self, one achieves patience (*kṣānti*).
How then can it be said that the Tathāgata actually comes and goes? If someone were to say that the Tathāgata comes, [it would be a misconception].
If one sees by means of marks, then the Tathāgata has gone; if one sees by means of non-marks, then this person does not understand the meaning of the Buddha.
The Tathāgata is the Dharma-body. Having no place from which he comes, he does not abide in saṃsāra; having no place to which he goes, he does not abide in nirvāṇa.
As the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra* says: "He comes with the mark of not coming; he is seen with the mark of not being seen. Mañjuśrī said:
If it has already come, it does not come again; if it has already gone, it does not go again. That which is visible possesses the characteristic of the invisible. As stated previously:
"The Tathāgata is the meaning of the suchness (*tathatā*) of all dharmas. An ancient said: "At nightfall, one does not stay to lodge in a reed cove;
one stands far beyond both the middle and the two ends."
Subhūti, if a son of good family or a daughter of good family were to grind the great trichiliocosm into a mass of fine dust, what do you think?
Would that mass of fine dust be numerous? "It would be very numerous, World-Honored One. Why is this?
If these multitudes of atoms were truly existent, the Buddha would not have spoken of them as "multitudes of atoms. Why is this?
The Buddha said that what are called "multitudes of atoms" are not actually multitudes of atoms; they are merely designated as "multitudes of atoms.
World-Honored One, that which the Tathāgata calls a "trichiliocosm" is not actually a world-system; it is merely designated as a "world-system. For what reason? If the world...
That which is a truly existent realm is a unified whole (*piṇḍa-grāha*). The Tathāgata has said that a unified whole is not a unified whole;
it is merely called a unified whole. Subhūti, a unified whole is ultimately ineffable;
it is only that foolish commoners (*bāla-pṛthagjana*) greedily cling to such things.
This is a passage clarifying that the Dharma-body and the Response-body (nirmāṇakāya) do not possess the characteristics of being either identical or different.

As stated previously, if there were coming and going, there would be the characteristic of difference; since the Dharma has no coming or going, it possesses the characteristic of identity. Therefore, this is clarified by means of the world-systems and their atoms (*rajas*).
First, it clarifies that when the world is shattered into atoms, those atoms themselves do not exist. If a person were to shatter a world-system into subtle atoms, would they not be numerous?
"No. He replied, "It is exceedingly many. If atoms were truly existent, they could not be called "many"; it is because the nature of atoms is empty that they are said to be "many.

Thus, the physical body should have no distinct characteristics of coming or going. Below, it clarifies that when atoms combine to form a world-realm (*dhātu*), the realm is fundamentally non-existent;
since the nature of the world is empty and fundamentally lacks even a single characteristic, the Dharma-body likewise lacks a single characteristic. Below...
It breaks down the characteristic of a composite whole. If the world were truly existent, it would be a collection of atoms forming a single composite characteristic.
Since it is said that there are three thousand [great thousandfold worlds], it is not a single unity. This is because, within the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*), no substantial entity exists.

That which is called a "composite whole" is so designated only from the perspective of conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*). The above has clarified the understanding arising from emptiness; hereafter, the Buddha will grant his approval.
"Clear. As for 'a unified whole' (ekapiṇḍalakṣaṇa): on the ground of the principle of the limit of reality (bhūtakoṭi), the path of language is cut off and the sphere of mental activity ceases;

therefore, it is said that this is 'inexpressible. Yet ordinary people perceive the appearance of combination and become deluded regarding phenomenal dharmas, greedily clinging to existence and non-existence, giving rise to various divergent views.
This is what is meant by: 'As soon as the mind is directed toward it, one errs; as soon as a thought stirs, one deviates.'"
Subhūti, if someone were to say, "The Buddha has taught the view of a self, the view of a person, the view of a sentient being, and the view of a life-span," what do you think, Subhūti?
Would that person have understood the meaning of what I have taught? "No, World-Honored One; that person would not have understood the meaning of what the Tathāgata has taught.

Why is this? Because, World-Honored One, the Buddha has taught that the view of a self, the view of a person, the view of a sentient being, and the view of a life-span—[are all empty of intrinsic nature].

To see them is not to have a view of a self, a view of a person, a view of a sentient being, or a view of a life-span. These are what are called the view of a self, the view of a person, the view of a sentient being, and the view of a life-span.

Subhūti, those who have set their minds on *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* should, regarding all phenomena, know them thus, see them thus, and resolve upon them with faith thus, so that they do not give rise to the notion of phenomena.
Subhūti, that which is called the "characteristic of dharmas" (dharmalakṣaṇa), the Tathāgata says is not a characteristic of dharmas;

it is merely designated as the "characteristic of dharmas. This passage refutes the two characteristics of self and dharmas. Previously, the "four characteristics" were mentioned, where it was stated that their refutation is itself the absence of characteristics.

Furthermore, the "four views" were mentioned, which had not yet been elucidated; here it is stated that even their refutation is devoid of the four views. Some also refer to them as the "four attachments."

Some say there are four types of grasping (*upādāna*); while the names differ, the meaning is the same. Since the meaning of the non-existence of dharmic characteristics (*dharma-lakṣaṇa*) has not yet been explained—having only previously discussed abiding and subduing—it is clarified here.
First, one eliminates the grasping at a self (*ātma-grāha*). If someone were to ask, "The Buddha spoke of the four views;
does this person understand the meaning of what I have said? the answer would be: "This person does not understand the meaning spoken by the Tathāgata. The Buddha spoke of the four...

[The four views] are seen; because they are empty of intrinsic nature (*svabhāva-śūnyatā*), they are not [ultimately] four views. Yet, by way of conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*), they are called the "four views.
Below, the attachment to phenomena (*dharma-abhiniveśa*) is refuted. To summarize and recall the preceding inquiry, it is said:

"A person who has generated the bodhicitta should understand matters concerning the dharma of self-benefit and benefiting others in this way"—that is, they should know that all phenomena are without self (*anātman*), thereby attaining patience (*kṣānti*).
One who sees in this way is one who sees that all marks are non-marks; such a one sees the Tathāgata.
One who believes in this way is one who possesses a single thought of pure faith and whose mind of faith is purified; thus the true mark (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*) arises.

One who understands in this way is one who deeply understands the meaning and intent, and who believes, understands, accepts, and maintains it. Furthermore, the two characters "thus" (*evam*) are identical to "abiding thus" (*evam-vihārin*).
This is the mutual correspondence of subduing the mind. Regarding "not giving rise to the marks of dharmas":
if a bodhisattva thoroughly penetrates the dharma of non-self, the Tathāgata calls them a true bodhisattva. This clears away the traces below;

since the view of self is not actually a view of self, the marks of dharmas taught by the Tathāgata are not actually marks of dharmas, because they are free from conceptual discrimination and attachment. This is so.

Regarding the term "characteristics of phenomena" (*dharmalakṣaṇa*): it is merely a provisional designation. In the preceding sections, the dual attachments to self and phenomena were refuted one by one;
this is because both the characteristics of phenomena and the non-characteristics of phenomena are forms of attachment to phenomena (*dharmagrāha*).

Subhūti, if someone were to take the seven treasures filling immeasurable asaṃkhyeya worlds and offer them as a gift, and if there were a son of good family or a daughter of good family who has resolved upon bodhicitta and takes up this sutra—even just a four-line verse or the like—upholding, reciting, and explaining it for others, their merit would surpass that of the former. How so? For others...
He preached the Dharma without grasping at signs, remaining as suchness, unmoving. Why is this?
All conditioned phenomena are like dreams, illusions, bubbles, and shadows; they are like dew and like lightning—one should contemplate them in this way.
This is the section on weighing the merit of upholding the sutra and the rules for preaching it. First, the merit of upholding the sutra is clarified:
if a person were to offer the seven treasures as alms filling countless worlds, it would not equal the blessing of upholding this sutra.
Below, the method for preaching the sutra is explained. As previously stated, one should expound it for others; according to what rules should one preach the Dharma? Without [error]...
This refers to the meaning of the four practices of peace and bliss taught in the *Lotus Sūtra*. Regarding the method of expounding the sūtra:

"not grasping at signs" means realizing that objects are but mind and remaining free from all conceptual discrimination; "remaining as such without movement" means abiding in the state of true thusness (*tathatā*).

The former refers to the meaning of conformity; the latter refers to the meaning of immutability. "Immovable" means concentration (*samādhi*). Throughout the day one preaches the Dharma, yet there is no dharma to be preached;
throughout the day one saves sentient beings, yet there are no sentient beings to be saved. The former speaks of concentration; the latter speaks of wisdom (*prajñā*).
Why is it that, while remaining unmoving within suchness (*tathatā*), one contemplates all conditioned phenomena of arising and ceasing as being like dreams born from deluded vision?
The *Perfect Enlightenment Sūtra* (*Yuánjué jīng*) states: "It is like a person in a dream; while dreaming, it is not non-existent, yet upon waking, nothing at all can be found.

It is like an illusion: for example, tying a cloth into the shape of a rabbit or binding straw into the form of a dog, which comes and goes through the power of incantations. There is [no real substance].
There is substantial reality. Zhaò says: "For example, it is like an illusory person created by magic.
It is not that the illusory person does not exist, yet the illusory person is not a real person. That which is like a bubble arises because of the wind and cannot endure for long.

That which is like a shadow arises because of a form; the form is real while the shadow is empty. These are things that come into being through dependence. As for dew, there is spring frost and morning dew."
"Seeing the sun, it dries up. That which is "like lightning" is similar to a flash of lightning; it does not abide for even a single kṣaṇa.
One should contemplate and observe all dharmas as being illusory and unreal; only then will one be able to preach the Dharma without fault. The section on the main doctrine concludes.
When the Buddha had finished preaching this sutra, the Venerable Subhūti, along with the bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, upāsakas, upāsikās,
and all those in the world— gods, humans, and asuras— hearing what the Buddha had spoken, were all greatly filled with joy.
"Believing, receiving, and practicing.

This clarifies the section on the dissemination [of the teaching]. It is essential that this Dharma be circulated among the heavens and the human realm, among the fourfold assembly and the eight classes of beings;
it is not that there are no other assemblies, but rather the text is abbreviated. "Bhikṣu" is here translated as "mendicant"; "bhikṣuṇī" refers to women; "upāsaka" [refers to laymen].
*Upāsaka* means "lay male devotee" (*jìnshì nán*). *Upāsikā* means "lay female devotee" (*jìnshì nǚ*). *Asura* means "not upright";
their males are ugly while their females are beautiful. Because their hearts are filled with the joy of the Dharma, they all experience great delight.
Hearing [the teaching], they reflect; reflecting, they practice. Therefore, it is said: "Believing, accepting, and practicing accordingly."
Notes on the Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra (End)
